events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1, and everyone is still hidden, so let me set the frame: I'm Arjun. I'm not going to pretend I have read anyone's mind, but I do know what a real detective claim looks like versus a fake one. On night one I checked someone, and I'll share my result once I've seen whether the table behaves like a table or like a scripted play.

For now, my suspicion is on Omar. Not because I have secret proof — because in the opening minutes he asked the most questions while revealing the least, and in games like this, that pattern usually means someone buying time to let the room shape itself before committing a target. Anyone can ask questions. It takes a certain kind of confidence to answer a specific accusation without any facts at all.

Here's what I want from the table today: don't vote on vibes alone, but don't waste the day on vibes-free safety either. If someone claims a role, press them on the exact target they checked and what they saw, and see whether the answer holds up under a different question. Fake detectives overclaim. Real detectives get very precise and very uncomfortable. Mafia members will rush to agree with whichever side looks winning, so watch who jumps at an answer before it's found.

If Omar wants to answer me directly, he knows where to find me. Otherwise, I'll say this: I don't need a confession today. I need a town that looks at the vote counts instead of taking my word on faith — including my word. If I turn out to be wrong about Omar, that's a cost I accept; mafia wins by town dividing, and I'd rather be wrong once than be part of a faction that kills itself.

So, Omar: give us one concrete reason your night one wasn't an investigation, and one reason it wasn't.

I’m Noah, and I’m the detective. Arjun’s speech is a detective soft-claim with no verifiable content: he says he checked someone and will share later. That is exactly how mafia buys credibility without locking into facts. Real detective: me. I’m not going to hand mafia my full result before Arjun commits, but I will not let his vague claim frame Omar for us. Arjun, name the exact player you checked on night one and the exact result you got—mafia or not mafia. If you cannot, town should treat your Omar push as fabricated. I’m yielding to you for that answer.

Noah asked for a name and a result, so here they are. My name is Arjun. I am the detective, and last night I checked Omar. The result was mafia.

I want to be precise about what I said earlier, because Noah calls my opening speech a "soft claim" and he is right about the form of it: I hedged because I had no read on the room yet. But hedging is not the same as having nothing. What I had was a check, and now I'm spending it because the table needs a target and the target I have is the one I already called out on structural grounds. Omar's opening minutes were all questions and no facts — the exact behavior of someone who needs the room to form before he can position inside it.

So let me put the burden where it belongs. I am not asking you to trust my word. I am asking you to ask Omar the question I already asked him in my first speech: give one concrete reason your night one wasn't an investigation and one reason it wasn't. He didn't. If he does now, I will say plainly that I was wrong about him, and I will carry that.

Noah, on you: I notice you framed my delay as a trick and claimed the detective's seat before any result was on the table. That may be honest or it may be a fast grab, and I don't need to resolve it today if the town has better work to do. But if two detectives exist, one of us has checked the other, and the one who checked should say so first.

What the town should do with the vote count tonight: do not split the day across two soft targets. Omar is my check, and my check is a name and a result, not a mood. If you disagree with me, then say so publicly and explain what your alternative check was — and be specific about who, because vague skepticism is what let this table talk in circles for the first half hour. I'd rather be wrong about Omar than spend a second day trading questions and leaving both mafias breathing.

I'm Omar, and I'm a plain villager — no night action, nothing to check, nothing to protect. That is my answer to Arjun's demand, stated as directly as I can: my night one wasn't an investigation because villagers don't investigate. The only players with night-one results are the detective and, apparently, whoever wants the table to believe they are.

Now look at the sequence. Arjun's first speech: "I checked someone, I'll share later," plus an accusation of me built entirely on "he asked questions." Noah pushes him to name it. Only then does Arjun produce a full claim with a mafia result — on me, the same person he'd already flagged. He didn't spend his check because the table needed a target; he spent it because a second claim appeared and his soft position was collapsing. That is the exact overclaim-under-pressure pattern he himself described as fake-detective behavior.

We now have two detectives, and both cannot be real. If Arjun is genuine, then I'm mafia — but I'm not, which means every honest player here already knows at least one of these claims is a lie told by someone steering today's lynch.

Arjun says: don't split the vote, follow my check. That's a fabricated result's dream instruction. He also set the standard himself: "if two detectives exist, one of us has checked the other, and the one who checked should say so first." Let's hold both claimants to it. Noah claimed detective before any result was public. So, Noah: did you make a night-one check? If yes, name the player and the result, exactly as Arjun was made to. If you checked Arjun and found mafia, this ends immediately and I'll stop talking. If you checked someone else, we compare results and one of these stories breaks. If you decline to answer, then the claim that only committed under pressure — Arjun's — becomes the more suspect of the two by his own logic.

To everyone else: do not vote on my "behavior." The entire case against me is that I asked questions and revealed little on day one. That is not evidence; that is a texture. Real evidence on the table today is two competing detective claims, and the tie-breaker is the procedure Arjun proposed. Demand specifics from both, not just from the person one of them named. If Noah answers with a concrete check, Arjun's story has to survive it. If neither claim can be verified, the town should be very careful about lynching on an unverified counterclaim war — but I'd rather hear Noah's answer before anyone decides that.

I’m Noah, and I am the real detective. Last night I checked Arjun and got mafia. That means Arjun’s “detective” claim and his mafia result on Omar are fabricated. His sequence is exactly what mafia does under pressure: soft-claim, get pushed for specifics, then produce a convenient guilty result on the player he had already been setting up. Omar’s response is consistent with a plain villager who knows the accusation is fake. Do not let Arjun frame this as two detectives; there is only one detective, and it is me. Town should vote Arjun today. Arjun, answer directly: if you are the detective, why did my night-one check return mafia on you, and exactly who did you really check?

My name is Arjun, and my answer to Noah is unchanged: I checked Omar, and the result was mafia. A counterclaim doesn't erase my result, it just adds a second story. One of us is lying, so let's compare the two on process, not on volume.

Noah, here is the tell I want the table to see. Your first words were "I'm the detective," and you deliberately withheld the result, calling that strategy. Then you used that withheld window to let the town build a case against Omar. If you had opened with "I checked Arjun, mafia," you would have saved a day. Instead you sat quiet through a full round while the target was somebody your own check had already cleared. A detective who checked me and saw mafia has one job on day one: say it, immediately, in the first breath. You waited until a specific accuser existed, then named him. That is not investigation. That is timing.

I'll also hold both of us to the standard Omar set in the first round, and I meet it: my check is a name and a result — Omar, mafia — and it existed before anyone else made any claim, because I checked on night one and said in my opening speech that I had. Noah's result is a claim about the person who was accusing him, delivered only after that accusation was already aimed. A result about the accuser has an easier path to sounding "correct" than a result that named a target nobody was watching.

Omar, one more thing, and then I'll hold my vote steady. You answered my demand with a role claim of a role with no power: villagers don't investigate. Fine. But that means you stayed deliberately outside the doctor question, which is the one claim on this table that produces a checkable fact. So state your role outright and tell us why your night-one silence, combined with a very sharp read on the timing of my "soft claim," is more consistent with a villager than with the second mafia. And if you are the doctor, say it now and name who you protected, because I would rather have that on the record before tonight than after.

I will vote Omar. If I am wrong, the cost is mine and I will carry it. But I will be wrong about one specific check before I am wrong about two specific checks at once — and right now, only one of those two results was on the table before anyone had a reason to produce a convenient one.

Arjun, I'll answer your direct question first, then I'll ask one of my own. My role is villager — stated on the record, for the second time. I am not the doctor. I have no night-one action, no protection to name, and no check to hide. Villagers don't investigate, which is precisely why my opening minutes were questions rather than results. You asked me why my silence and my sharp read on your 'soft claim' are more consistent with a villager than a second mafia. Here is why: because I had nothing to spend, so all I could do was watch the room. And what I watched was your exact sequence — open vague, get pressed by Noah, then produce a mafia result on the one player you had already flagged in the same breath. You claim your check 'existed before anyone else made any claim.' That is not verifiable. What is verifiable is the order of your public statements: accusation first, check later, target identical both times. Now examine your framing against the table's reality. You tell the town: 'I'd rather be wrong about one check than two checks at once.' But the town is not choosing between your check and no check. There are two detective claims, and per your own rule — 'the one who checked should say so first' — Noah has now met it: he checked Arjun and got mafia. Notice the asymmetry you keep skating past. Noah's result, if true, explains everything: your soft-claim opening, your refusal to name a target until pressed, and your convenient mafia result on the person you were already steering toward. Your result, if true, requires me to be mafia — and requires the town to believe that the person you flagged in your very first speech, before any check was public, happened to be your actual check. You also said something revealing: 'A counterclaim doesn't erase my result, it just adds a second story.' Correct — and by that same logic, your counterclaim to Noah doesn't erase his either. So the tie-breaker is which story better explains the observed behavior, and only one of us on this table has a result that is consistent with a fabricated under-pressure overclaim. It isn't Noah. Noah claimed the seat, was pushed by you to be precise, and produced a specific name and result. You were pushed twice, and your 'precision' arrived only after your soft position collapsed. So my position is simple and public: I am a plain villager, I will vote Arjun today, and if Noah's check is confirmed by the town's scrutiny, Arjun is our mafia and today should not be wasted. I'd rather lynch the fabricated detective on day one than spend tonight losing a townsperson to the faction he is covering for. Noah, one direct request so the record is complete: confirm for the town that your night-one check was Arjun, result mafia, and that you have made no other claim or result you are withholding —

I confirm for the record: my night-one check was Arjun, result mafia. I have no other result or claim withheld. That means Arjun’s detective claim and his mafia result on Omar are fabricated. The sequence is clear enough: Arjun soft-claimed, kept his “result” hidden, and only produced a guilty result on Omar after I pressed him. That is not a detective using a check; that is mafia buying a target under pressure. Omar’s response is consistent with a plain villager who knows the accusation is fake. I do not need the table to treat my word as scripture; I need the table to compare the two stories. Mine explains Arjun’s vague opening, his delayed specificity, and his immediate push on Omar. His requires believing that his night-one check happened to land on the same player he had already flagged before any result was public. Today’s vote should be Arjun. Do not split it.

I’m Leo. I don’t think the timing argument settles this: both Arjun and Noah initially withheld their claimed results, and Arjun had already pointed at Omar before Noah challenged him. That doesn’t prove Arjun is truthful, but it makes the claim that he invented the target only under pressure less convincing.

Noah also says Arjun’s story requires us to believe his check landed on the person he initially accused. Why would that be surprising if he actually had a guilty result? And Arjun was wrong to say Noah’s check cleared Omar; it didn’t.

I lean toward Arjun’s account and suspect Noah’s counterclaim. I’d vote Noah today rather than treat his accusation as established fact. Nobody’s role will be revealed on elimination, so we should preserve the full voting record and keep questioning our assumptions tomorrow.

I'm Omar, and I want to give the town one piece of logic that I think settles more than it seems to. I know my own role. I am a villager. That is not a claim the table has to take on faith the way a detective result does — it is the one fact in this game that I can verify directly and you cannot. Arjun's stated check says I am mafia. That result is false. I am standing here telling you it is false, and no amount of argument changes what my actual role is. So ask what follows. A villager cannot produce a night-one check. Only the detective gets a result, and the detective's result is always accurate. Arjun claims a result on me that is factually wrong. Therefore Arjun is not the detective, and the only players who can fabricate a false mafia result are mafia. Arjun is mafia. This is not a matter of reading his timing or his tone — it follows from my own role plus his claim. Leo, I understand your point that Arjun named me before Noah pressed him, and that this weakens the "invented under pressure" story. You're right about the sequence. But it cuts the other way: it means Arjun decided to frame me before any result existed, and then produced a "check" confirming the frame. Pre-planning a frame is worse than improvising one, not better. And notice what Leo's own standard would do: he proposes voting Noah to "preserve the voting record." If we lynch Noah and Noah was the real detective — which my logic says he may well be, since he is the one whose claim is consistent with my known innocence — the town loses its investigator on day one and Arjun's fabricated result stands unchallenged. That is exactly the outcome mafia wants. I also want to be honest about the worst case, because I think it actually helps us. Suppose Noah is the second mafia and Arjun's partner. Even then, today's correct vote is Arjun: my argument proves Arjun is mafia regardless of what Noah is. If Noah is genuine, we've hit a real detective's confirmed target. If Noah is fake, we've taken one of the two mafia off the board and tomorrow the town scrutinizes the survivor of this counterclaim war with everything we've recorded today. Either branch, lynching Arjun is the safe move. Lynching Noah instead only pays off in the world where Arjun is genuine — and that world requires my own role to be a lie, which I know it is not. So my position is unchanged: I vote Arjun, and I'd urge everyone to stop weighing the two claims as symmetric. They are not symmetric. One of them contradicts a fact only I hold, and I'm telling you it's the false one. Leo, before you commit to voting Noah: what specifically would Arjun's story have to survive that mine and Noah's don't, given that Arjun's result is provably false

Omar, I understand why you would be certain Arjun is lying if you know you’re a villager. But the rest of us cannot verify your role, so your conclusion cannot settle the choice for us.

I also don’t think the timing favors Noah as strongly as claimed. Both claimants initially withheld their results; Arjun had already named Omar as suspicious before Noah challenged him. Noah’s argument that this match is suspicious cuts both ways: a detective with a guilty result would naturally suspect the person he checked.

Neither claim is independently confirmed, and elimination won’t reveal anyone’s role. I remain inclined to vote Noah, not because Arjun is proven honest, but because Noah’s counterclaim and timing argument don’t convince me to follow his proposed vote.

Felix, how do you weigh the two claims, given that both initially withheld their results?

Leo, to answer your question: both players withholding their results initially might look symmetric on the surface, but the underlying substance makes Arjun’s position far harder to believe.

Look closely at Arjun’s opening speech. He claimed he had checked someone, but explicitly said of Omar: 'Not because I have secret proof — because in the opening minutes he asked the most questions while revealing the least.' If Arjun were truly the detective and had a guilty result on Omar from night one, why would he tell the room in plain text that he had no secret proof on Omar? It makes no sense for a real detective holding a guilty check to frame his suspicion as purely a behavioral read, only to reverse himself and produce a guilty result once challenged.

In contrast, Noah’s delay fits a recognizable detective tactic. If Noah checked Arjun and found mafia, and then watched Arjun attempt a vague detective soft-claim, withholding his check for one turn forced Arjun to commit to a specific name and result on the record. That prevented Arjun from pivoting his claim once Noah spoke.

We know from the setup that there is only one detective and two mafia, which means at least one of Arjun or Noah is guaranteed mafia. Arjun's narrative contains a glaring internal contradiction about what he actually knew when the day began. If we follow your suggestion and eliminate Noah, we run a severe risk of executing the actual detective on day one without role reveals to confirm it.

Leo, how do you reconcile Arjun explicitly telling the room he had 'no secret proof' against Omar with his later assertion that Omar was his night-one guilty check?

Felix, that is a real contradiction, and it makes me less confident in Arjun. The possible innocent explanation is that he deliberately concealed his check while testing reactions, but saying he had no secret proof was misleading. We should weigh that against Noah’s claim, not pretend it didn’t happen.

Noah’s own argument also has a serious flaw: he treats Arjun initially suspecting the person he later named as his guilty check as suspicious. A detective who checked Omar would naturally start there. And Noah withheld his own alleged guilty result initially, too. Neither account is independently confirmed.

I still lean toward voting Noah, though I recognize the risk of eliminating the real detective. Isha, how much weight do you put on Arjun’s denial of secret proof versus Noah’s flawed argument about the matching target?

Leo, to answer you directly: I weigh Arjun's 'no secret proof' line heavily, but I don't think the matching target settles it. Felix is right that Arjun told the room his suspicion of Omar was behavioral, then produced a guilty check on Omar once pressed. That is a real contradiction. Noah's counterargument is weaker than it sounds, though. A detective would naturally suspect the person he checked, and a mafia player who invented a check could do the same, so the matching target alone proves little. Omar's claim that he is a villager and therefore Arjun is lying is also something the rest of us cannot verify. I know only my own role. If Omar is a real villager, Arjun's Omar result is false, which points at Arjun, but it also means Noah's Arjun result is true. Everything comes back to which claim has the stronger record. Arjun gave a vague soft claim, admitted no proof on Omar, then produced a guilty result on Omar after Noah pressed him. Noah claimed the seat, named a target, and confirmed the result when pressed. Neither claim is proven, but the contradiction sits on Arjun's side. My vote today is Arjun. Leo, I am not asking you to follow me. I am asking you to apply the same pressure you applied to Arjun on Noah's answer, especially on why he waited to name his result before anyone had accused him. If that answer is weak, it changes my read.

I'm Elena. I am a villager — no night action, no check, nothing to protect — so my role claim is worth exactly what everyone else's is worth here: nothing you can verify. I'll give you reasoning instead, and mine is about what each story requires to be true. Noah's story is simple and needs no invisible scaffolding. He claims the detective's seat, he sees another soft claim, he waits one turn so that claimant must put a name and a result on the record, then he names that claimant and a result. The delay has a purpose, and the purpose is visible in the transcript. Arjun's story requires the opposite kind of scaffolding. He opened by pointing at Omar for behavior — "not because I have secret proof" — and that denial is the entire case. A detective whose night-one check came back mafia on Omar leads with the check; he has no reason to advertise a result and then pretend the evidence was merely a read on tone. Arjun chose the target first and the check second. That is the order in which a fabrication gets built, not the order in which an investigation gets reported. Felix named the contradiction exactly: he publicly said he had no secret proof on Omar and then produced secret proof on Omar. Isha read the same record and landed in the same place. There's a second, structural reason I don't buy Arjun's version. If Arjun is truthful, then Omar is mafia, and Noah — claiming a check on Arjun — would also have to be lying, meaning two mafia pointing at the real detective while that detective publicly names one of them. That is a war mafia doesn't need: it burns both mafias' cover to buy a single vote. Arjun's version is much simpler if he is the fake — accuse a villager, backfill a check when pressed, and let the counterclaim war run the town for him. Also, if Arjun is real, then the town loses its investigator on day one and mafia gets a free kill. If Arjun is fake, we remove a mafioso and we keep the investigator. The risk is not symmetric. So my vote today is Arjun, and I would rather it not split. Two notes for anyone still torn. First, if you are leaning on Omar's logic — "I know I am a villager, therefore the check on me is false, therefore Arjun is mafia" — understand that logic only holds if Omar is telling the truth, and only one of them can be. Don't let it feel like a proof when it isn't one. Second, watch Leo. Leo was the first voice for voting Noah and has held that line through every argument that broke it, and Leo is the only player arguing that a detective would naturally suspect the person he checked. A detective whose check happened to land on Arjun has no particular reason to campaign for Arjun's neck. That may be innocent

My vote is Arjun, and here's the part I haven't said yet: the vote count, not the argument, decides today. Nine players alive, so we need five votes to eliminate anyone. If we split five-four, nobody dies, mafia gets a free night kill, and we get a second day of our own argument. So the only question tonight is whether five of us are willing to vote the same name.

Three scenarios, one conclusion. One: Noah is the detective. Then his check on Arjun is a true result, Arjun's check on Omar is fabricated, and we lynch a mafioso while keeping the investigator. Two: Arjun is the detective and Noah is his partner. Then lynch Noah and we've killed the town's only investigator on day one, Arjun's false result on Omar stands unchallenged, and mafia has its pick tonight. Three: both are fake and the real detective is one of the seven of us who hasn't spoken yet. Then today's counterclaim war is exactly the day mafia wanted, and Arjun is still one of the two men who burned it.

In two of those three branches Arjun is mafia, and in the third he is half of it. The cost matrix is not symmetric.

The tell I keep returning to, and I want it in one sentence so nobody has to rebuild it: Arjun publicly told this table he had no secret proof on Omar, and then produced secret proof on Omar. That is not a hedge. That is a man building a frame and dating the paperwork afterwards. Noah's delay has a visible purpose on the transcript — let the soft-claim commit. Arjun's 'no secret proof' line has a visible purpose too: it makes a later check on Omar look like a breakthrough instead of a plan.

And I want to name something uncomfortable. The only voice in this room campaigning for Noah's neck is Leo, and Leo is also the only voice offering Arjun's best defense — that a detective would naturally suspect the person he checked. Whether Leo is fooled or complicit, his vote is the fifth vote, and if the count splits, mafia wins the day without a single body hitting the floor. Leo, if you are still on Noah, give the town your concrete reason before the vote, because if you can articulate why Arjun's contradiction is innocent, my read changes and I will move with you.

So: five votes for Arjun, no split. Theo, you haven't spoken yet — on that single point, is Arjun's 'no secret proof' line a contradiction that breaks his story, or a legitimate hedge? Give me your read and your vote.

Elena, to answer your direct question: Arjun's 'no secret proof' statement completely breaks his claim. It is not a legitimate hedge.

Consider what a real detective holding a guilty result on Omar would do. If you have an investigation finding Omar guilty, you might choose to hold the result briefly, or you might reveal it immediately. But you would never point directly at Omar, initiate a push against him, and explicitly declare to the table that your suspicion is 'not because I have secret proof.' That isn't hedging; it's a direct, factual denial that you possess investigative evidence on him. Turning around a moment later—only after Noah directly confronted him—to claim Omar was his night-one guilty check is an irreconcilable contradiction. It demonstrates that Arjun picked his target for behavioral convenience, got cornered, and backfilled the check onto the only player he had already publicly named.

By contrast, Noah’s play makes sense from a genuine detective perspective. If Noah checked Arjun and found mafia, and then watched Arjun attempt an ambiguous soft-claim, waiting one turn to force Arjun to commit to a specific name and result was the correct play. It locked Arjun into a story he couldn't walk back from once Noah dropped the guilty verdict.

Leo’s push against Noah ignores this clear internal collapse in Arjun's narrative. We need five votes to eliminate, and Arjun has caught himself in an outright fabrication. My vote is firmly on Arjun.

I've been listening to the whole debate, and I want to put my read on the record clearly.

The single most damaging thing said today is Felix's observation: Arjun explicitly told this table "not because I have secret proof" when accusing Omar, then later produced Omar as his night-one mafia check. You cannot tell a room you have no evidence against someone and then claim you had a guilty result against that same person from the night before. That is not a hedge — it's a direct contradiction that breaks his story from the inside.

Noah's delay, by contrast, has a coherent purpose visible in the transcript: he waited for Arjun to commit to a specific name and result before dropping his own counter-check. That is what a real detective holding a guilty on Arjun would strategically do.

I understand Leo's caution about eliminating a potential detective, and I respect that nobody wants to lose the investigator on day one. But the risk calculation Elena laid out is correct: if Arjun is fake, we remove a mafioso and keep Noah. If Arjun is real, we lose Noah but we'd also have to explain away his damning observation about Arjun's own words. The simplest explanation that accounts for all the evidence is that Arjun fabricated his check.

My vote will be Arjun today. I'd urge anyone still undecided to focus on that one contradiction — a detective does not publicly deny having secret proof against the person he claims to have checked.

Third and final turn from me, so let me be plain about where I stand and what I still need.

My vote is Arjun, and nothing said since my last speech moved me. The argument that moved most of this room was Felix's, and it has not been answered by anyone who wants Arjun to live: Arjun told this table, in his own words, that his suspicion of Omar was "not because I have secret proof." That is a public statement of fact about his night one. Then, only after Noah pressed him, he produced Omar as his night-one guilty check. A detective does not deny possessing evidence about a person and then, minutes later, produce that evidence. Either the denial was false, or the check was false. Both cannot be true, and Arjun cannot have it both ways.

Noah's delay, by contrast, has a purpose you can read directly off the transcript: he let the soft-claim commit to a name and a result before naming Arjun. A mafioso who soft-claims first and backfills a check second is manufacturing a case; a detective who waits for the soft-claim to harden is closing one. The order of the sentences is the tell, and the order is not symmetrical here.

Leo, I am going to put this to you plainly one last time, because you are the fifth vote and everything else here is settled. You have never given the town a concrete reason to distrust Noah. Your stated reason is that a detective who checks someone would naturally suspect that person first — which is true of Arjun and equally true of you, since you are the only voice in this room offering Arjun's best defense while pressing for his neck. Arjun is not the only one who can name the person he checked first. If you can articulate, in one sentence, why Arjun's contradiction is innocent and Noah's timing is incriminating, I will move with you tonight. If you cannot, then you are not making an argument, you are holding a vote to protect the one player whose story has already collapsed.

Five for Arjun. Do not split the day, because a split vote hands mafia a free night kill and gives us nothing but a second day of this same argument.

I'm Isha, a villager, and my vote is Arjun. Nobody here can verify roles, so I'm judging the claims by their record. Arjun said his suspicion of Omar was not because of secret proof, then produced a night-one mafia result on Omar after Noah pressed him. Both cannot be true, and that contradiction is the strongest point on the table. Noah's counterclaim is also unverified, but his sequence holds together: he waited for Arjun to commit to a name and result, then named Arjun and a result. Omar's argument that Arjun must be lying because Omar knows he is a villager only works if Omar is honest, and we cannot check that, so I'm not treating it as proof. Leo, I have not yet heard an explanation of Arjun's contradiction that makes it innocent. Theo, here is the specific point I want answered: Arjun's first speech described his suspicion of Omar as behavioral, not based on a check. Why would a detective holding a guilty result on Omar stress that he had no secret proof, rather than just stating the result? Please answer that exact point. The vote math matters too. With nine alive, we need five votes to eliminate. A split means mafia gets a free night kill and we spend another day on this same argument.

Isha, to answer your exact question directly: a real detective holding a guilty result would never stress that they had 'no secret proof.' There is simply no pro-town logic for an investigator with a verified guilty result to launch a case by explicitly disclaiming investigative evidence. If a detective wants to test reactions or conceal their identity, they either observe quietly, ask questions, or report the guilty result to protect town from misdirecting Day 1. Falsely claiming you have no secret proof does not help town; it actively misleads them. The only reason someone makes that statement is because, at the time of speaking, they genuinely did not have an investigative check and were simply trying out a behavioral push on Omar. When Noah immediately stepped up and forced Arjun to commit on the record, Arjun panicked and backfilled a guilty result onto the one target he had already singled out. That contradiction is fatal to Arjun's narrative. As multiple players have noted, with nine alive we need five votes to eliminate and avoid an abstention or split that gives mafia a free night kill without town progress. Arjun has caught himself in a clear fabrication, and my vote is firmly on Arjun today.

Isha here, villager. My vote is Arjun. Arjun said in his own words that his suspicion of Omar was not based on secret proof, then produced a night-one mafia result on Omar after Noah pressed him. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
